item.title: Exploring Deep Learning Models for Environmental Optimization in Morel Mushroom Cultivation
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Morchella mushrooms (Morchella spp.) are highly valued edible fungi due to their distinctive flavor and medicinal benefits. However, their artificial cultivation remains challenging because growth is extremely sensitive to environmental fluctuations and complex interactions among soil, moisture, and temperature. Conventional control approaches are largely manual, inefficient, and unable to respond dynamically to microclimatic variations, resulting in unstable yields. To address these limitations, this study proposes a Hybrid Deep Environmental Optimization Framework (HyDEOF) that integrates Deep Belief Networks (DBN) with an Adaptive Neuro‐Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) for intelligent environmental regulation during Morel cultivation. DBN models nonlinear patterns from sensor data, while ANFIS enables real‐time adaptive control of humidity, CO2 concentration, and soil temperature. Experimental results from controlled cultivation chambers demonstrate that HyDEOF improves yield consistency by 21%, reduces energy consumption by 19%, and enhances substrate moisture retention by 17% compared with conventional systems, highlighting its potential for sustainable and efficient Morel production. Key stressors influencing Morel cultivation include humidity fluctuation, CO2 imbalance, and soil temperature variability, critically affecting fruiting stability. The methodology utilizes sensor‐based environmental data collection using DBN‐based feature extraction and ANFIS‐based adaptive control within a closed loop system. This approach is tested using experimental studies that evaluate environmental stability, productivity, and energy consumption.

item.title: GIS‐MCDA and Uncertainty Analysis for Underground Dam Candidate Zone Prioritization in the Beyşehir and Çumra Subbasins
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Underground dams can support subsurface water storage in water‐scarce basins, but preliminary siting requires the integration of heterogeneous hydrogeological, environmental, and planning factors together with an assessment of spatial decision uncertainty. This study develops a GIS‐based sequential spatial decision‐support framework for prioritizing underground‐dam candidate zones in the Beyşehir and Çumra subbasins of the Konya Closed Basin, Türkiye. Twenty‐one raster factor layers representing hydrological, hydrogeological, geological, topographic, soil, land‐use, climatic, accessibility, and settlement conditions were standardized and integrated using hierarchical AHP weights and weighted linear combination over 2,092,998 valid pixels of an 84.68‐m grid. Criterion redundancy and criterion influence were examined before aggregation: the largest variance inflation factor in the primary criterion set is 4.18, and decomposing the variance of the composite score shows that its spatial pattern is driven mainly by five soil and geology layers, which carry 31.6% of the total weight but produce 77.6% of the spatial variation. The continuous suitability surface was classified using quantile five‐class classification, with observed equal‐interval classification as a control; within‐one‐class agreement between the two classifications was 85.03%, with 45.51% exact agreement. AHP weight uncertainty was examined through 500 Monte Carlo perturbation scenarios, and cells exceeding a fixed reference score in at least 80% of scenarios, covering 254,887.07 ha, were carried forward. After protected land was removed, 1267 contiguous zones were extracted; 156 exceeded a 50 ha minimum‐area threshold and 16 were non‐dominated on suitability, exceedance frequency, and compactness, covering 19,461.56 ha. Groundwater depths at 33 wells showed no significant association with the suitability score and are used as a plausibility check. The framework links criterion redundancy and influence, classification stability, weight uncertainty, spatial contiguity, and planning constraints within a sequential decision‐support workflow.

item.title: Synthesizing Geographical Semantics and Large Language Model for OD‐Based Trajectory Captioning
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Trajectory captioning aims to represent trajectories in natural language texts, providing a human‐friendly approach to understanding and utilizing trajectory data. Previous trajectory captioning methods relied on manually defined rule templates to describe trajectories, failing to accurately and comprehensively capture the trajectory semantics. To address these issues, this paper synthesizes the semantics of the origin and destination (OD) points of trajectories with large language models (LLMs) to improve trajectory captioning. The proposed method first designs a trajectory context augmentation module that enriches the trajectories' context using the spatial information from Point‐of‐Interest (POI) distributions and human travel data from check‐in records. The method develops a geographical semantic‐based reasoning module that constructs a time‐subcategory graph and trains a POI matching module to capture the geographical semantics of the trajectories. Finally, a trajectory decoding module is developed, which leverages LLMs and the Chain‐of‐Thought inspired strategies to generate trajectory captions. Extensive experiments show that the proposed method outperforms baseline methods on both lexical‐overlap and semantic‐alignment metrics. This paper explores a new approach for trajectory semantics representation and provides a methodological reference for the text generation tasks in various geographical applications.

item.title: Continuous Merging of Buildings Considering Functional Semantics and Global Optimization
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Continuous generalization is a key technique for achieving continuous scale representation of map features, and the continuous merging of buildings is a crucial component of this process. Existing methods for continuous building merging predominantly focus on smooth geometric transitions, lacking explicit modeling of functional semantics and a search mechanism for globally optimal merging paths. To address this gap, this paper proposes a continuous building merging method that integrates functional semantic information with a global optimization strategy. The method first identifies building functions using POIs and AOIs data. Building aggregation patterns are then recognized based on Gestalt theory and serve as target constraints. Subsequently, a dynamic A* algorithm is employed to determine the globally optimal merging sequence, where the merging cost comprises distance, shape, functional semantics, and importance. Finally, buildings are merged sequentially through Delaunay triangulation filtering and orthogonalization algorithms. Experimental results on a Zhengzhou dataset show that the proposed method produces optimal merge sequences in 89.2% of cases and reduces the total merging cost by 12.6% over the best baseline, achieving continuous building merging with superior morphology and semantics.

item.title: Unsupervised Patch‐Based Ecoregion Classification in Austria Using DEM‐Derived Features, Deep Learning, and Climate Data
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Digital elevation models (DEMs) are widely used to characterize terrain and support applications ranging from geomorphology to environmental management. While traditional analyses rely on handcrafted geomorphometric features, advances in machine learning enable richer, data‐driven representations of topographic surfaces. In this study, we present a multi‐source feature fusion approach that integrates statistical descriptors of elevation, derived terrain attributes, deep features extracted via a ResNet encoder, and climate variables from weather datasets. Using 5175 randomly sampled 1km×1km$$ 1\;\mathrm{km}\times 1\;\mathrm{km} $$ patches, we generated a comprehensive feature set and applied unsupervised clustering to identify ecoregional units. Results indicate that combining DEM‐derived features with climate data produces clusters that are both quantitatively robust, as indicated by internal validity indices, and exhibit meaningful spatial distribution when compared with known ecoregions.

item.title: Comparative Analysis of Influencing Factors for Diverse Urban Renewal: Evidence From Beijing's Built‐Up Areas
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Investigating the influencing factors of urban renewal and their differences across renewal types helps optimize resource allocation. Existing studies have analyzed the influencing factors of multiple types of urban renewal, but have not yet identified the differences in the effects of these factors across different renewal types or tested the statistical significance of such differences. Therefore, this study selects multiple influencing factors from three dimensions—location environment, social services, and economic foundation—and constructs a multinomial logistic regression model to analyze the effects of these factors on four types of urban renewal: commercial and office renewal, public service facility renewal, park and green space renewal, and residential renewal. Meanwhile, Wald tests are used to examine the statistical significance of the differences in the effects of each influencing factor across different renewal types. The results show that: (1) land price is an important influencing factor for all types of urban renewal, while factors such as the distance from renewal points to major roads and the density of transportation facilities exhibit differentiated effects; (2) in the comparison of statistically significant differences in influencing effects, the relationships among different renewal types mainly present three patterns: “single comparison,” “single radiation,” and “multiple intersection”; and (3) a comprehensive comparison of the influencing factors of different urban renewal types and their differences indicates that urban renewal is jointly guided by the dual cores of government and market forces, driven by both ecological and social demands, and promoted through interactions among multiple stakeholders.

item.title: Cartographic Storytelling for the “2Ws and 1H” in Flood Perception: An Interactive and Time‐Varying Evacuation Plan for the General Public
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Disaster maps play an essential role in disseminating risk information to the general public. However, conventional disaster maps usually present static flood information, making it difficult to translate flood risk information into individualized and actionable evacuation decisions. This article adopts the idea of cartographic storytelling and proposes a time‐varying coupling approach that links flood simulation outputs with dynamic evacuation route planning for residents. Specifically, the proposed approach updates building risk states as the flood evolves and simultaneously plans routes to shelters according to current conditions and potential risks, thereby transforming complex spatiotemporal flood dynamics into tailored evacuation route recommendations that answer the “2Ws and 1H” questions of public evacuation, namely when to evacuate, where to go, and how to reach a shelter. Finally, a section of the Rhine River in Bonn, Germany, is selected for experimental analysis. The experimental results show that the proposed approach not only presents flood information but also provides actionable insights throughout the evolution of the flood, supporting the public to understand dynamic flood risk changes and take clearer and more timely evacuation actions during flood events. Our findings could support the development of interactive evacuation tools for residents during floods, as well as rescue management and disaster education.
